blocks.text: **The task.** Given a 2D grid, visit every cell in column-major order — top to bottom down column 0, then down column 1, and so on — collecting the values into a flat list.
Trace it: down column 0 gives 1 then 4; down column 1 gives 2 then 5; down column 2 gives 3 then 6.
Swap the loops. Columns on the outside, rows on the inside. The indexing expression `grid[r][c]` does not change at all — only the order in which the pairs are generated.
Notice we now read the column count **once**, from `grid[0].length`, instead of per row. We have to — the outer loop is over columns, so there is no current row to ask.

This quietly assumes every row is the same length. For a genuine rectangular grid that is fine. For a ragged array it will read past the end of a shorter row, so check the shape first if that is possible in your input.
**Time: O(R x C)** — the same count of cells, visited once each. Identical big-O to the row-major version.
**Space: O(R x C)** for the output.

In a row-major language — which is almost certainly yours — this traversal jumps `COLUMNS` elements forward on every step of the inner loop. Each jump likely lands in a different cache line, so the CPU waits for memory far more often.
Same complexity, measurably slower. Write column-major traversal when the **problem** requires that order, never as a stylistic choice.
